The story of Gautam Dev—a 61-year-old IIT Kanpur alum facing severe financial strain after a 2-year job search in the US—is a sobering reminder of today’s harsh tech reality.
Even with two decades of software engineering experience, senior professionals are being squeezed by a mix of ageism, hiring freezes, and rapid AI disruption. Traditional experience alone no longer guarantees security.
For seasoned tech professionals navigating this tough market, survival requires a fast pivot:

* Shift to Fractional Roles: Bypass automated job boards. Target short-term contracts, freelance gigs, or fractional consulting for mid-sized firms that need mature technical oversight.

* Adopt AI, Don't Build It: You don't need to create AI models. Master AI-assisted coding tools (like Copilot or Cursor) to prove your development speed matches modern expectations.

* Monetize Legacy Systems: Thousands of enterprises still run on foundational architectures. Position your deep experience as a rare asset to maintain or migrate these systems.

* Activate Alumni Networks: Cold applications are failing. Lean heavily on university networks and former colleagues for warm introductions directly to hiring managers.

* Protect Your Runway: If local costs are unsustainable, downsize or relocate early to preserve savings before a crisis hits.

The tech landscape has changed, but experience still holds immense value when paired with adaptability.

Your workforce has a ceiling. 
Your competitor's is about to disappear.

Hours in the day. Headcount. Hiring time. Training time. Sick days.

That's your limit. You've been running a business inside it for years.

AI doesn't have one.

10,000 calls in 30 minutes. Thousands of documents read before lunch. The same job done at 2am on a public holiday.

That isn't a faster staff member. It's a different kind of workforce.

I saw a post on LinkedIn recently. A business got a negative review because a lead came in at 2am and nobody got back to them until 9:30am.

Petty? Sure. Ridiculous? Probably.

But it's real. And it's solved by AI.

It can call or text that lead the second it lands. Or you decide how each lead's treated. AI handles it now, or it waits for a human.

You choose. The ceiling's gone either way.

And most businesses are still asking "is it as good as Sarah?"

Wrong question. Dangerous question.

While you're benchmarking it against one person, someone else is doing the work you can't afford to do. Quoting every lead. Following up every enquiry. Reading every contract.

If you're building or selling AI... stop pitching "cheaper than a person". That's a race to the bottom. Sell what a business can do once the ceiling's gone.

If you're buying AI... stop asking what it replaces. Ask what you turn away today because you don't have the capacity. That's where the money is.

The opportunity isn't doing the same work cheaper. It's doing work you could never afford to do before.

But aim it badly and you just make mistakes faster.

Know your business first. Then remove the ceiling.

The hardest part of moving evaluation from humans to AI isn't the model. It's the operation around it.

I've seen this from both sides. As COO of a Trust & Safety services company, I helped build a human review operation from scratch to 1,200 agents across five major platforms. More recently, I spent almost two years on the operations side of large-scale search evaluation as it moved from human-led to AI-led.

Three things I didn't expect:

1. The humans don't go away. Their job changes. They stop rating and start setting the bar, auditing the AI and owning the hard cases. It's a different skill set, and most operations aren't hiring for it yet.

2. Your vendor model breaks first. Contracts, staffing plans and quality checks are all built for volume. When the volume moves to AI, all three stop fitting, often before anyone notices.

3. Calibration becomes the job. Every time the AI improves, the bar moves, and someone has to keep telling you where it moved.

Trust & Safety and content review are next. The teams that come out ahead won't have the best model. They'll have redesigned their operations around it.

If you run a human-data or T&S team: which of these are you seeing, and what am I missing?

The Future of Identity and Access Management (IAM): From Access Control to Strategic Identity Security
Identity and Access Management is evolving rapidly as organizations adopt cloud technologies, AI-driven solutions, and Zero Trust security models.
From a market and architecture perspective, IAM is no longer just about provisioning accounts and managing access. It is about building a secure, scalable, and intelligent identity ecosystem that aligns with business goals while reducing security risks.

Key IAM trends shaping the industry:
--> Identity Governance & Administration (IGA): Strengthening access certifications, role management, and compliance through solutions like SailPoint.
--> Identity Security & Zero Trust: Moving toward continuous verification, least-privilege access, and risk-based identity decisions.
--> Cloud Identity Management: Simplifying identity lifecycle management across hybrid and multi-cloud environments using Microsoft Entra ID and Okta.
--> Identity Threat Detection: Improving visibility into excessive privileges, orphaned accounts, and suspicious identity activity.
--> AI-Driven Identity Automation: Leveraging intelligent automation to streamline Joiner-Mover-Leaver processes, access reviews, and governance workflows.
--> Converged Identity Security: Bringing IGA, PAM, SSO, MFA, and access management together to create a unified identity security strategy.
--> My perspective: The next phase of IAM will be defined by how effectively organizations connect identity governance, automation, cloud security, and Zero Trust principles to deliver both stronger security and a better user experience.
The real opportunity lies in moving beyond reactive access management toward proactive, risk-aware identity security.

I'd love to hear from IAM professionals, architects, and security leaders:
What do you believe will have the biggest impact on IAM over the next 2–3 years — AI-driven identity security, Zero Trust, or unified identity governance?

What if an AI agent could do more than understand what happened inside an enterprise?
What if it could explore what could have happened instead?
What if demand dropped 20%?
What if a major customer defaulted?
What if a supplier failed?
What if interest rates increased?
What if production capacity declined?
What if hiring froze?
What if costs suddenly increased?
This is the idea behind Xpert Systems’ Connected Enterprise What-If datasets.
A Connected Enterprise provides an interconnected business world where customers, suppliers, employees, products, contracts, operations, transactions and financial records are linked across time.
The What-If version takes this further.
We can introduce a scenario or shock and allow its consequences to propagate across the enterprise.
A supplier disruption can affect procurement.
Procurement can affect inventory.
Inventory shortages can affect production or fulfillment.
Fulfillment problems can affect customers and revenue.
Revenue changes can affect cash flow.
And ultimately, the consequences flow into the financial statements and general ledger.
Now an AI agent can reason about more than:
What happened?
It can investigate:
What happens if this changes?
Which processes are affected?
What are the second- and third-order consequences?
What happens to revenue, costs, cash and operations?
What actions could management take?
Which decision produces the better outcome?
This creates powerful environments for AI model training, AI agent training, scenario analysis, counterfactual reasoning, evaluation and benchmarking.
Instead of testing whether an AI agent can retrieve information, we can test whether it can reason through an enterprise under changing conditions.
That is a much harder—and much more valuable—AI problem.
And we don't only build Connected Enterprises.
Xpert Systems also buys and licenses real-world enterprise data that can legally be used for AI training, evaluation, benchmarking and research.
Historical data, operational data, transactions, ERP, CRM, accounting, procurement, manufacturing, supply chain, engineering, HR, documents, contracts and emails may all be valuable.
Building AI models or AI agents that need enterprise-scale What-If environments?
Or does your organization have real enterprise data it has the legal right to license for AI?
Let's talk.

Breaking into Web3 and AI Agents as a builder has completely shifted how I think about trust and software.

For the past week, as part of the RiseInWeb3 #Agentmaxxing cohort, I’ve been building Scout (web3-scout-agent)—a side-project combining Next.js, Gemini 2.5 (@google/genai), and Viem on Base.

Most AI apps are stateless wrappers. The real shift is agentic workflows—AI with tool-calling loops, runtime memory, and an autonomous financial primitive.

The problem I kept running into:
Traditional recruitment is full of resume noise, while Web3 hiring suffers from manual, high-friction escrow and delayed milestone payouts.

What Scout does differently:
It’s an autonomous, dual-sided AI agent with an embedded EVM wallet.
1. For recruiters: It writes high-signal technical briefs and audits a candidate's 0x smart contract deployment history instead of a PDF.
2. For candidates: It matches on-chain proofs to roles and handles transparent, single-line autonomous gas/escrow settlements.

How the Agentic Loop Works:
Instead of a human copying-and-pasting between ChatGPT, Etherscan, and a multisig, Scout operates as a closed-loop runtime:
1. Intention Routing: Evaluates if the user is an employer or candidate.
2. Tool-Calling (@google/genai function declarations): Proactively invokes verify_onchain_talent to inspect 0x deployment history or get_wallet_amount.
3. Autonomous Execution (viem): Signs and broadcasts escrow milestones directly from its embedded EVM wallet, returning a strict 1-line transparent audit log (Paid X ETH...).

Building this made one thing clear: Web3 is the native financial layer that AI agents have been missing. 

Without an on-chain wallet and deterministic verification, agents are just expensive advisors. With them, they become economic actors.

This is Week 1 of the journey. In the coming weeks, I’m looking at ZK identity integration and x402 payment protocols.

If you’re building at the intersection of AI agents and EVM—or if you have feedback on how you handle on-chain reputation—I’d love to connect.

Green card curbs may barely dent Indian IT. Here's why that matters for US tech leaders.

Every time US immigration rules tighten, the same question comes up: what happens to tech delivery?

The answer is shifting. Over the last decade, how companies hire tech talent has changed:

🔹 Global delivery is the default now. Offshore and nearshore teams carry the bulk of the work, not just support.
🔹 Local hiring has grown. More US roles are filled by US-based talent, with niche skills brought in on demand.
🔹 Hiring models are mixed. Full-time, contract-to-hire and contract are used side by side to match each role.

For CTOs and engineering leaders, the takeaway isn't to worry about policy. It's to make sure your talent strategy doesn't depend on a single pipeline.

The companies that come through these shifts best have:
✅ A blend of onshore and offshore capacity
✅ Partners who can move fast on niche skills in AI, data and cloud
✅ Hiring that is flexible on the model, without lowering the quality bar

At New York Technology Partners (NYTP), this is what we do every day: help US companies build tech teams that hold up through these shifts. That means full-time, contract-to-hire or contract, backed by a global delivery model.

Policy will keep changing. Resilient talent strategies don't have to.

On tasks AI suits, consultants using it finished 25% faster. On one it didn't suit, they were wrong more often than the ones without it 
A team from Harvard Business School, Wharton, MIT, Warwick and Boston Consulting Group gave 758 consultants realistic work, with GPT-4 or without it.
On tasks inside what AI does well:
→ 12.2% more tasks finished
→ 25.1% faster
→ Quality rated 40% higher
On a task built to sit outside it:
→ Without AI, 84% got the right answer
→ With AI, 60 to 70% did
One of the authors, Ethan Mollick, called the result "the 'Jagged Frontier' of AI". Some work sits inside the line, some outside, and you can't see the line from where you stand.
The idea for any business: sort the work before you hand it over.
→ AI drafts, a person checks: emails, meeting notes, FAQs, checklists
→ AI helps, a person decides: pricing, hiring, contracts, anything with a number
→ A person does it: complaints, negotiations, judgment calls
The study's trap task shows why the checking matters. Only the consultants who compared the spreadsheet with the interview notes reached the right answer.
What it does for daily operations: the drafting work runs faster, and the check catches the confident mistakes before a customer sees them.
Which task on your list is AI drafting today?
I'm posting one practical AI idea for running a business every day. Follow so you don't miss the next one.

While I sympathise with the sentiment behind them, I deeply disagree with some of the arguments against publishers who use machine translation (MT) and generative AI (GenAI) systems.

The basic argument goes something like this: Modern MT/GenAI systems are developed and used in often unethical ways. Therefore, publishers who adopt such systems are unethical, and people should boycott such publishers.

The implicit message in this argument is that publishers should continue to hire human translators for translating books.

Consider, though:
(1) Do publishers tend to compensate translators adequately?
(2) Do publishers hire translators primarily based on merit?
(3) Are publishers cultivating a linguistically diverse market where translation based on human creativity is encouraged?

One could plausible answer these questions as follows:
(1) Publishers generally don't compensate translators adequately, as studies by the Authors Guild and CEATL, among many others, strongly suggest.
(2) Publishers make hiring decisions frequently based on cronyism and/or on whether the candidate is privileged enough to translate a book at impossibly low pay or even for free.
(3) Publishers often require translations to be simple and easy to read so as to make the book (or the product) appealing to a mass market and also be eligible for as many big awards as possible, while genuinely creative translations are marginalised and rejected as "experimental".

If the above is an accurate description of the state of mainstream publishing, why are people suddenly upset to hear that many publishers consider translators to be eventually replaceable by MT/GenAI systems?

For those of us with skin in the game, are we scrutinising publishers on their compensation levels and hiring practices? When we receive offers and contracts which are exploitative, cronyist or classist, are we pushing back and rejecting them or are we accepting them while making excuses to ourselves? Are we pushing back against the overwhelming demand for easy-to-read, standardised prose styles, or are we promoting genuine linguistic diversity?

I know that the above is easier said than done, but I also know that many translators, though in the minority, are pushing back on such practices when many others aren't.

My take on the recent controversies is that if translators are serious about preventing the deterioration of our profession, we need to stay focused on compensation, cronyism, classism and the dominance of a certain type of standardised prose styles as the core issues. More of us need to start pushing back on these norms and be prepared, if need be, to forego the privilege of translating the books we love.

If a publisher and/or a division or a team within a publisher pays its translators well, hires based on merit and encourages a variety of non-conventional prose styles, such a publisher should be supported and cheered on regardless of whether it is incorporating MT/GenAI systems into its business.

Last week, after seven brilliant years, I left Shelter. In that time, I was lucky to grow and learn so much as we built the community organizing programme, campaigned through a pandemic, led the fight for renters rights, two general election campaigns, and so much more. There's way more than a LinkedIn in post worth of lessons, but here are a few of my major take aways:

1) My definitive answer to the question 'can NGOs organize?' is yes. They can, should and must be into building power with the communities they serve to make change happen. I'll die on this hill. 

2) Building power takes time, change takes time, and you have to persist. Stop running one year 'pilots', stop hiring people on six month contracts. Stop paying consultants to come and go. Put core funding into hiring and training staff, resourcing power building activity, and commit.

3) The most important bit of your theory of change is running the experiment to test your theory. At the end of it all, action is oxygen. So act.

4) Be willing to fail, and then learn from it.   So many times we asked ourselves, 'what might happen if...?' and then we went and found out, and learned from every time we fell on our faces. It was great. 

5) Hiring the right people is make or break. People who are confident, but doubt themselves, that are thoughtful but driven to act, that are brave but careful, that are optimistic that things can get better but cynical that it can happen without hard work, and that can do serious things with good humor, are hard to find. If your recruitment process finds these specs of gold, hire them!

6) Know your people! Whose power are you trying to build? Do not define this by who it isn't, don't do it on (just) people who support your cause. They're not just people against the same thing as you, or people who are just angry. Shared values, experiences, ways of working, and mindset all matter. Describe who it is you want to campaign with until you can walk up to that person in real life, then crack on

7) Teach people! Equip people with the skills, knowledge and motivation to make change happen. We incorporated lessons from people all round the world into our work and never stopped learning.

8) Invest in building resilience. In this work keeping people going is absolutely crucial. There's no one doing this better than Stephanie W. and Ariel Lew Ai Le W. at Act Build Change. Work with them, learn from them. I know I have.

9) When it comes to politicians, always ask for more than you think you can get. Sure, concede when you have to, but always ask for what your people really need.

10) Seek out people with different perspectives, skills, and knowledge and learn from them. It is people with differences, working together, that really makes change happen.

And if you ever have a CV land on your desk with a red Shelter chevron on it, you should hire that person. They are probably the best there is at what they do, are awesome to be around whilst doing it.

Did you change who is qualified to run it?

Oracle and BorderPlex announced that Project Jupiter will use Bloom Energy fuel cells to fully power its AI data center campus, supported by up to 2.45 GW of installed capacity.

The distinction matters: this is a planned primary power source, not equipment waiting for a utility outage. That should change the recruiting conversation.

“Critical facilities experience” tells us where someone worked. It does not establish whether they have managed the operating conditions your new power design creates.

Someone who has maintained emergency generators may bring valuable experience. That experience still needs to be examined against continuous generation, controls, maintenance coordination and recovery requirements.

Neither does a vendor service agreement answer every staffing question. Leadership must establish what the provider owns, what the site team must understand and what happens when the problem crosses that boundary.

The question is not whether the candidate has data center experience. It is whether that experience matches the facility you are actually building.

YOU HAVE INVESTED IN A NEW POWER STRATEGY.

The old model was reactive: a new dataset arrives, you catalog it, you classify it, you write a policy, and then you enforce it. The latency between arrival and enforcement is where every failure lives. The new model, as confirmed by the latest industry guides, is anticipatory. You embed the governance logic directly into the data's provenance before it ever enters a pipeline. The policy is not applied after the fact. It is inherited.

The non-obvious consequence is that the data catalog is no longer a passive inventory. It is a runtime execution layer. Every field, every schema, every transformation carries its own governance contract. When a query arrives, the system does not check a separate policy database. It reads the contract embedded in the metadata. The governance decision is made at the same speed as the query itself. There is no handoff. There is no review queue.

Here is the practical reality. A team that builds a machine-learning model on customer data in 2026 cannot afford a three-day approval cycle. The model's training window is hours, not days. The teams that succeed are the ones that have stopped treating governance as a separate review gate and started treating it as a pre-compiled set of permissions that are evaluated at line speed. They have moved from policy as a document to policy as a runtime constraint.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the one who can write the most comprehensive governance framework. It is the one who can design the metadata schema that makes policy enforcement a self-executing property of the data itself. I specialize in this. I build the embedded governance layers that let organizations scale regulated data operations without introducing a human-in-the-loop for every access request.

The hardest problem in Data Governance right now is not defining what is allowed. It is engineering a system that can prove, at the exact moment a query executes, that the correct policy was enforced, without adding any measurable latency to the data path. If your organization is scaling AI on sensitive data, what is the one policy you have not yet embedded into your metadata layer that is currently causing your biggest trust gap?
